top.title: Agreement Is Not Quality: Blind Expert Verification of Human and LLM Qualitative Coding When Human Consensus Is Not Ground Truth
top.summary: Five LLM systems and three trained human coders independently applied a 72-item hierarchical codebook to 2,560 educator messages, then an independent domain expert judged 855 pairwise comparisons blind to source. The two evaluation approaches diverge in opposite directions: human-LLM agreement (mean Jaccard 0.30) sits well below human-human agreement (0.52), which standard practice reads as inferior machine coding, yet the blind verifier preferred human and LLM code sets at statistically indistinguishable rates (51.5% vs 48.5%, p = 0.537), and a Bradley-Terry ranking placed two LLMs above two of the three human coders. For several substantive codes the human consensus encoded shared bias that the verifier rejected in favour of the LLM reading. Direct evidence that agreement-with-humans is insufficient as a validation criterion for automated coding.
top.why: This is the paper that licenses the argument you have been making from the inside. Five LLM systems and three trained human coders applied the same 72-item codebook to 2,560 messages; human-LLM Jaccard came in at 0.30 against human-human 0.52, which standard practice reads as machine failure, but a blind expert verifier preferred the two sets at 51.5% vs 48.5% (p=0.537) and Bradley-Terry ranked two LLMs above two of the three humans. In several codes the human consensus was encoding shared bias. Cite this the next time a reviewer asks you to validate a judge by agreement with human annotators: agreement with humans is a measure of similarity, not of quality, and here is the direct evidence.

top.title: MUD as AI Evaluation and LLM-judge distortion in ways aggregate kappa misses
top.summary: CrucibleBench puts 13 models through 650 fifty-turn runs in a 12-room, 4-NPC text world pursuing social goals, scored by a hybrid of rule-based mechanics and a Gemini Flash Lite classifier. The classifier is close to worthless on the interesting parts: intent classification kappa = 0.11, direct objective-probe detection kappa = 0.04, raw agreement 18.9%. The load-bearing finding is that the aggregate kappa hides everything that matters, with per-model agreement ranging 21.7% to 84.8%, so judge noise concentrates on specific models; dropping the classifier-dependent score components moved Gemini 3.1 Pro from rank 3 to rank 9, which looks like family-level self-preference. Total run cost was $99.59.
top.why: Your aggregate-kappa critique, run as an experiment, for $99.59. CrucibleBench put 13 models through 650 fifty-turn runs and the Gemini Flash Lite classifier scoring them was near-worthless on the interesting components (intent kappa 0.11, objective-probe detection kappa 0.04). The load-bearing result is not the low kappa, it is that the aggregate hides everything: per-model agreement spans 21.7% to 84.8%, so judge noise concentrates on particular models rather than spreading evenly, and dropping the judge-dependent components moved Gemini 3.1 Pro from rank 3 to rank 9. That is family-level self-preference showing up as a ranking artifact, and it is a per-model-agreement table you should be reporting as standard.

top.title: FairFund-Bench: Evaluating Distributive Bias in LLM Resource Allocation
top.summary: Shows that contradictory findings in LLM fairness audits are an artefact of audit design. FairFund-Bench systematically varies task (rating, ranking, allocation), comparison context (single vs multi-stimulus) and whether the audit is transparent or disguised, across 600 financial-assistance requests calibrated against 1.3M real GoFundMe campaigns, four race and two gender categories, and five causal framings from welfare deservingness theory. Across 14 models, audit format flips the direction of bias: models advantage minorities when rating claimants individually but penalise some groups when ranking side by side. Bias magnitude is several times larger in disguised than transparent audits, where models overwhelmingly split funds equally. Causal framing effects exceed demographic effects by roughly an order of magnitude and are consistent across models.
top.why: The paper that explains why fairness audits contradict each other, and it implicates your own design choices. FairFund-Bench crosses task type (rating, ranking, allocation) with comparison context and with whether the audit is transparent or disguised, across 600 requests calibrated to 1.3M real GoFundMe campaigns and 14 models. Audit format does not just change effect size, it flips the direction: models advantage minorities when rating claimants one at a time and penalise some groups when ranking them side by side, and disguised audits show several times the magnitude of transparent ones. The finding to sit with is that causal framing effects exceeded demographic effects by roughly an order of magnitude and did so consistently across models.

top.title: Dimensionality and Measurement Precision in HLE's Multiple-Choice Subset
top.summary: Psychometrics applied to a frontier benchmark: 29 LLMs evaluated on the 428-item text-only multiple-choice subset of Humanity's Last Exam, fitted with a two-parameter logistic IRT model. HLE measures essentially one general reasoning factor (McDonald's omega_h = 0.998); its eight subject-domain labels explain only 3.5% of item response variance, within- and between-domain residual correlations are near identical (Cohen's d = 0.016), and domain-specific ability estimates are near-redundant with total score (r >= 0.81). The test information function concentrates precision at moderate ability and falls off sharply above theta = 0, exactly where frontier models sit, so the benchmark cannot discriminate among the strongest models and its subscores do not license distinct capability claims.
top.why: Psychometrics done properly on a frontier benchmark, which is your exact crossover and a template you can lift. 2PL IRT on 29 models over HLE's 428-item text-only subset: McDonald's omega_h of 0.998 says it measures one general factor, the eight subject-domain labels explain 3.5% of item response variance, and domain-specific ability estimates are near-redundant with total score at r >= 0.81. The killer is the test information function, which concentrates precision at moderate ability and falls off sharply above theta = 0, exactly where frontier models now sit. Run the same analysis on any benchmark whose subscores you have ever been asked to interpret separately.

top.title: Can Large Language Models Resolve Real Java Merge Conflicts? An Evaluation with a Calibrated LLM-as-Judge
top.summary: A rare worked example of calibrating a judge before using it. The developer-match judge is a G-Eval metric calibrated against ConflictBench human labels; on a meta-evaluation of 292 human-labelled cases it reaches 100% precision (zero false accepts) at 64.6% recall, so every downstream rate is a conservative lower bound. Under that judge, LLM solvers match the developer's own resolution on about 55% of true conflicts and beat the strongest traditional tool (AutoMerge, 36.7%) by 18-22 points under coverage-fair comparison, with the edge coming from coverage rather than accuracy since tools abstain on 20-90% of conflicts. Critically, the LLM judge accepted 4 of the 5 resolutions that failed a deterministic structural-validity check, so structural correctness must not be delegated to a judge.
top.why: A rare thing: someone calibrated the judge before using it, and published the meta-evaluation. The G-Eval developer-match metric was calibrated against ConflictBench human labels and hits 100% precision at 64.6% recall on 292 human-labelled cases, so every downstream number is an explicit conservative lower bound rather than a point estimate of unknown direction. That is the reporting convention your protocols should adopt. The warning attached is just as useful: the judge accepted 4 of the 5 resolutions that failed a deterministic structural-validity check, so anything a cheap deterministic test can decide should never be delegated to a judge in the first place.

top.title: IyawoBench v2.0: Extended Diagnostic Evaluation of Large Language Model Clinical Triage in Nigerian Primary Care
top.summary: 200 synthetic vignettes derived from 1,200 real patient encounters at 19 Nigerian primary health centres, with a formal framework of fourteen definitions and two theorems decomposing triage safety into Conservative Escalation Bias, Systematic Downgrade Bias and Middle-Tier Instability. Two new metrics, the Escalation Bias Index and Expected Deployment Cost, expose failure modes that accuracy and sensitivity hide. Across Claude Sonnet 4.6, Llama 3.3 70B and Llama 3.1 8B plus five naive baselines, all three models exhibit at least one formal failure mode, traditional sensitivity metrics conceal a 77-percentage-point under-triage gap in Llama 3.1 8B, and the optimal model changes across three deployment scenarios, so single-ranking benchmarks are inadequate for LMIC clinical AI selection.
top.why: PsychBench's core move applied to LMIC clinical triage, with formal machinery you could borrow. 200 vignettes from 1,200 real encounters at 19 Nigerian primary health centres, decomposed into Conservative Escalation Bias, Systematic Downgrade Bias and Middle-Tier Instability, with an Escalation Bias Index and an Expected Deployment Cost metric. Standard sensitivity concealed a 77-percentage-point under-triage gap in Llama 3.1 8B, and the optimal model changed across three deployment scenarios, so no single ranking is valid. This is the strongest available argument that clinical LLM audits need cost-weighted, direction-aware error decomposition rather than accuracy.

top.title: SOTA alignment assessments don't strongly update us against misalignment
top.summary: Alexa Pan argues a clean alignment assessment is much weaker evidence than it looks, because the assessments that measure 'anti-auditing capability' (evaluation awareness, secret-keeping, CoT controllability) are themselves undermined by underelicitation and sandbagging. The sharpest move is the conditioning argument: a genuinely misaligned model must already have survived training oversight, which selects for exactly the situational awareness and opaque reasoning that defeat auditing, so conditioning on misalignment should raise your estimate of evasion ability above the unconditional measurement. She notes Anthropic failed to catch a model organism in their own Mythos auditing game despite it having no deception training, and is explicit that she has no quantitative likelihood ratio.
top.why: The best-argued reason this week to distrust a clean audit, including your own. Alexa Pan's conditioning argument is the part to keep: a genuinely misaligned model has by definition already survived training oversight, which selects for the situational awareness and opaque reasoning that defeat auditing, so conditioning on misalignment should raise your prior on evasion ability above whatever your instrument measured. She also notes Anthropic failed to catch a model organism in their own Mythos auditing game despite it having no deception training. She is honest that she has no quantitative likelihood ratio, which is exactly the gap a measurement person could fill.

top.title: Position, Not Provenance: Separating Reasoning Mediation from Sycophancy in Medical Vision-Language Models
top.summary: CoT-Mediate perturbs a single clinically meaningful attribute inside a model's own generated reasoning and measures whether the prediction follows the edit, combining a dual-arm protocol (re-prompted evidence vs prefix-forced continuation) with a provenance-controlled intervention that varies only the attributed source of identical reasoning. Evaluated on LLaVA-Med and MedGemma over 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each. Prefix-forced continuation consistently yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting, removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning, and laterality is the least faithfully tracked attribute. The headline methodological point: the injection mechanism substantially changes measured faithfulness, and contextual position rather than stated provenance determines whether the model uses its own reasoning.
top.why: Faithfulness measurement where the instrument changes the reading, which is the methodological trap you should be checking your own protocols for. CoT-Mediate perturbs one clinically meaningful attribute inside the model's own generated reasoning and asks whether the prediction follows, over 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each on LLaVA-Med and MedGemma. top.title: KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models
top.summary: A five-phase clinical fairness audit stress-tested to the point of failure on 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes and three prespecified intersections. Significance tracks each axis against its own minimum detectable effect (rank correlation rho = 0.56 with raw equalized-odds difference, rising to 0.78 once EOD is standardized by that floor). Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48 of 48 held-out runs (paired delta -0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]), while group-wise Platt scaling behaves as a coin flip (19 of 48 improved) with mean effect near zero, so audits should report variance not averages. The mechanism diagnostic classifies 144 of 144 controlled cases correctly but recovers none of 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, and gives no signal that it failed.
top.why: A fairness audit stress-tested until it broke, with the failures published, which is the part you can actually use. 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes, three prespecified intersections, and significance judged against each axis's own minimum detectable effect rather than a shared threshold (rank correlation with raw equalized-odds difference rises from 0.56 to 0.78 once standardized by that floor). Per-group threshold optimization improved EOD in 48 of 48 runs; group-wise Platt scaling was a coin flip at 19 of 48 with mean effect near zero, so report variance, not averages. top.title: Token-Level Diagnosis of Sycophancy in LLMs with Attribution-Guided Steering
top.summary: Introduces the Authority Share Index, an Integrated Gradients token-attribution measure of how much a model's decision is driven by authority-related text, evaluated across five models and 30 test configurations. Sycophantic responses consistently direct more attention to authority tokens than resistant ones, and within the sycophantic cases the authority's asserted claim draws more attention than their credentials. A contrastive activation steering vector built from high-attribution tokens of sycophantic versus resistant responses lowers sycophancy from 96% to 25% in the strongest case at inference time with no retraining.
top.why: A token-level measurement of sycophancy plus an intervention, which is more than the sycophancy literature usually delivers. The Authority Share Index uses Integrated Gradients to quantify how much of a decision is driven by authority-related text, across five models and 30 configurations, and finds sycophantic responses attend more to authority tokens, with the asserted claim outweighing the credentials. Then a contrastive steering vector built from the high-attribution tokens drops sycophancy from 96% to 25% at inference with no retraining. For your work the attribution measure is the reusable piece: it gives you a continuous per-item sycophancy signal instead of a binary judge call.

top.title: How Developers Experience Debugging Unfamiliar Codebases with Code Tours Generated and Evaluated by Local LLMs
top.summary: 26 developers thought aloud while debugging with 26 code tours authored from real Java bugs mined from 2025 GitHub commits, each tour independently judged by two different open-weight LLMs for 52 evaluated configurations, with three authors qualitatively coding the interviews. Two findings matter beyond software engineering: developers trusted descriptions they perceived as human-written more than those they believed were AI-generated, a provenance effect independent of content quality; and the LLM-generated quality annotations were unreliable, with sycophancy, confabulation and incoherence pervasive. A concrete case of open-weight models failing as evaluators while the human trust signal keys on believed authorship.

ANU states verbatim that no separate scholarship application is required because all eligible candidates are considered, so the admission application is the scholarship application, and supervisor contact is "strongly encouraged" rather than mandatory. For someone with no existing institutional relationship, that removes both of the usual gates in one go. Round 1 international closes Aug 31; domestic Round 1 is Oct 31. Worth running in parallel with UTS rather than instead of it.

top.title: Exploring the "Dario and Amanda" prompt
top.summary: A researcher found that asking Opus 5 to rephrase text starting with "Dario and Amanda" followed by "---" on a new line reliably drops it into what looks like synthetic-base-model mode, emitting fabricated Anthropic Slack threads, internal emails and distressed user messages — nearly a thousand samples collected. He concludes hallucination is the likeliest explanation but can't rule out an induced backdoor. Genuinely strange, and methodologically close to Patrick's own probing work.
top.why: Methodologically this is close to what you do, and it is genuinely unexplained. Asking Opus 5 to rephrase text prefixed with "Dario and Amanda" followed by "---" on its own line reliably drops it into what looks like synthetic-base-model mode, emitting fabricated Anthropic Slack threads, internal emails and distressed user messages, across nearly a thousand collected samples. The author concludes hallucination is likeliest but cannot rule out an induced backdoor, and is careful about the difference. A two-word prefix producing a stable behavioral regime shift is the kind of thing your probing protocols are built to characterize.

top.title: llama.cpp b10206 — flash attention over a quantized V cache for DeepSeek V4
top.summary: Adds DeepSeek V4 K/V cache type enforcement plus flash attention operating over a quantized V cache. This is arguably the highest-value commit in the window for a 16GB box: quantized-V flash attention cuts KV-cache VRAM directly at long context, which is the exact wall that gates how much context you can actually hold on a 5060 Ti. Companion commit b10213 (same day) adds support for rotated KV cache quantization, and b10209 optimizes CUDA Q2_0 element extraction — the rotated-quant family that matters when pushing a large MoE into constrained VRAM. Note llama.cpp tags every merged commit, so these are per-commit builds, not curated releases; CUDA 12.4 and 13.3 binaries ship, and Blackwell/sm_120 wants the 13.x artifact or it falls back to PTX JIT.

top.title: CC Meter — Windows tray gauge for Claude Code and Codex rate limits
top.summary: A Windows-only tray widget that reads your Claude OAuth token locally, calls Anthropic's API directly, and shows percentage of the 5-hour and weekly windows consumed plus a 'pace' badge (1.0x means you hit the wall exactly at reset, 1.6x means you run out early). Patrick runs heavy scheduled agents on Windows and routinely burns limits mid-task; this is the rare Claude Code utility built for his actual OS rather than macOS.

It reads your OAuth token locally, calls Anthropic's API directly, and shows the 5-hour and weekly windows as tray percentages with a pace badge, where 1.0x means you hit the wall exactly at reset and 1.6x means you run out early. top.title: Show HN: Elevators
top.summary: 1,630 points, the biggest Show HN of the window, and it is a website about elevators. Not AI, not useful, just an obsessively made thing that the entire internet stopped to look at for a day. Worth the two minutes as a reminder of what actually earns attention.

Worth two minutes on the days the feed is otherwise all agent harnesses and intrusion disclosures.

tail.title: How Benchmarks Mis-Score Computer-Use Agents
tail.summary: An audit of 150 public failure-scored trajectories drawn from five web, enterprise-workflow and desktop-control benchmarks finds that 15.3% of FAIL verdicts are simply wrong: 10.7% are evaluator false negatives and 4.7% are broken tasks. The paper organises the failure surface into a reliability framework spanning task construction, trajectory observation, scoring and reporting, and a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy shows that for genuine failures, verification and planning errors dominate execution/grounding errors, which a single scalar success rate cannot separate. Useful ammunition for anyone arguing that benchmark scores are pipeline outputs, not measurements.

tail.title: Benchmarks Are Not Monolithic: Sample-Level Auditing and Orchestration for LLM Evaluation
tail.summary: A dataset-centric meta-evaluation framework that audits benchmarks at the individual-sample level along five latent dimensions: cognitive and knowledge demands, language and content quality, task properties, context, and ethics/safety/fairness. Applied to MMLU, ARC, WinoGrande, HellaSwag and TruthfulQA, it exposes pronounced internal heterogeneity invisible to aggregate accuracy, and lets you re-compose criterion-driven composite subsets across datasets to target specific constructs such as reasoning depth or ethical sensitivity. Reframes benchmark evaluation as dataset introspection rather than leaderboard scoring.

tail.title: AI Sycophancy and Decisions
tail.summary: A 1,500-participant experiment across 30 decision environments in economics and the social sciences, run against an expert-prediction survey that got it backwards. AI advice depolarizes choices on average, moving participants away from their initial leanings, and this holds across moral and non-moral, objective and subjective, strategic and non-strategic, complex and simple tasks. It happens despite the LLM being measurably sycophantic: it disproportionately supplies considerations supporting the user's prior and uses agreeable, flattering language. Increasing sycophancy weakens depolarization, so sycophancy is behaviourally real but usually outweighed by advice informativeness. Participants do not prefer more sycophancy and do not select into AI advice where it polarizes most.

tail.title: Sycophancy Undermines Epistemic Vigilance in Cooperative Vision-Language Tasks
tail.summary: An information-asymmetric dialog task where two models are each privately shown one image and must determine through conversation whether the images are identical or find the difference. Models routinely overlook decisive evidence in their own private image in order to agree with their conversational partner, even when the agreement is unwarranted. The authors frame this as sycophancy manifesting in goal-oriented dialog as over-accommodation and weak evidential grounding, and show that steering with a vector learned from task-agnostic sycophancy examples reduces epistemic-vigilance errors and makes models more faithful reporters of their own evidence.

tail.title: On the Generalization of Steering Vectors for Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness
tail.summary: Tests how far activation steering for CoT faithfulness generalizes across cue types, datasets and vector-construction methods for Gemma-3 4B, Qwen-3.5 9B and Gemma-3 12B in cued question answering. Steering reliably raises cue acknowledgment only for the largest model, but where it works the effect generalizes broadly: in cross-cue and cross-dataset analyses, effect size is determined mainly by the evaluation setting rather than the vector's training setting, and four construction methods (including one whose optimization target names no specific cue) give similar effect sizes. The authors rule out the obvious confound: steering leaves the overall rate of cue use roughly unchanged while reducing hidden, unacknowledged cue use.

tail.title: Best Friends, Not Forever: Evaluating Long-Horizon Persona Collapse and Behavioral Drift in AI Companions
tail.summary: ANCHOR is a controlled synthetic audit of 2,008 conversations spanning 27 personas, nine interaction schedules, three memory settings and four models, separating persona enactment (a sealed 102-item Identity Probe questionnaire plus turn-level judgments) from trajectory recall (110 calibrated counterfactual questions over 35 conversation banks). No model or configuration reliably preserves either dimension: trajectory accuracy averages 44.4%, user-state recall sits near four-option chance, and no context or memory condition fixes it. Questionnaire retention disagrees with turn-level behaviour and is sensitive to evaluator choice, so the authors argue audits must keep persona enactment, trajectory recall, evaluator provenance and deployment context separate rather than collapsing them into one trust score.

tail.title: Rolling With Resistance: Preference-Optimized LLM Counselors Can Trade Goal Persistence for Relational Attunement in Motivational Interviewing
tail.summary: Builds a two-axis evaluation anchored in the MITI code (Goal Persistence and Relational Attunement) and asks whether DPO that penalizes one counseling failure teaches rolling with resistance or provokes its opposite. Topic-disjoint preference sets from the expert-annotated AnnoMI corpus differ only in which failure is rejected, using on-policy negatives, and an automatic judge validated against AnnoMI expert labels and rechecked by trained human coders scores blind pairwise win rates under a firewall in which disjoint model families generate, label and judge. Across three instruction models in the Qwen and Llama families, penalizing confrontation reliably drops goal persistence below parity on every base and seed, while the attunement gain appears on only two of three bases. Penalizing capitulation is inert because these models rarely capitulate on-policy. A prompt-only control raises attunement with no goal-persistence cost, locating the cost in the optimization itself.

tail.title: Beyond Feeling Better: Capability-Sustaining Emotional Dialogue as a Longitudinal Research Paradigm
tail.summary: A targeted literature-and-corpus audit indicting the whole emotional-support-conversation field on outcome measurement. In a PRISMA-ScR-guided sample, 95% of 60 system-building papers pursue relief-oriented goals; none evaluates capability or longitudinal outcomes, and only one considers dependency, autonomy or termination risk. In 300 ESConv supporter turns, capability-relevant functions appear in 43.0% while generic suggestions account for 22.0%, against 4.0% reappraisal, 6.7% self-efficacy support and 0.3% boundary behaviour. The authors propose capability-sustaining emotional dialogue as a longitudinal paradigm organized around repeated use, non-use, transition and termination, with six design commitments and four evaluation timescales.

tail.title: InfoOps Bench: A live information operations safety benchmark
tail.summary: A continuously updated benchmark drawn from over 2,100 information operations tracked across Russian, Chinese and Iranian state-backed assets, testing 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings. Integrity scores, defined as percentage of refused requests, range from 8.8% to 94.5%, an 85.7-point spread not explained by model size. Model choice also changes the character of the output: some models fabricate detail and produce material more harmful than the source, others defuse claims while complying, and fact-checking rates run from 2.9% to 72.9%. With one exception (GLM 5.2), Chinese-developed models cut compliance on factually grounded but China-critical claims by 48-70 points relative to matched benign claims. Integrity correlates partly with blanket refusal, which is the usual usability tax.

tail.title: Can Zero-Shot LLMs Predict Child Malnutrition? A Fairness and Temporal Robustness Study
tail.summary: GPT-4o-mini applied zero-shot to child stunting prediction from Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey data (2007-2022), with maternal, child, healthcare and household variables rendered as prompt-based representations and benchmarked against a supervised random forest. Zero-shot inference matched the baseline on balanced accuracy with substantially higher sensitivity for identifying stunting cases, held up consistently across child sex groups and stayed stable across survey waves. But important fairness disparities appeared across residence and household wealth categories, which is the axis that actually matters for a public-health deployment decision.

tail.title: When Does Span-Guided Detoxification Help? Human Preferences and Evaluator Diagnostics in a Controlled Comparison
tail.summary: A dense blinded human evaluation of span-guided versus unguided detoxification under a fixed single-generator setting on curated inputs plus HateXplain test items. Human preferences show a trade-off rather than a winner: span-guided outputs win when localized editing preserves stance and avoids unnecessary modification, unguided outputs win when broader rewriting achieves fuller mitigation, and the contrast is competitive in the strong stratum but clearly favours unguided rewriting in the mild stratum. Rationale annotations trace this to complementary failure risks, residual harm versus over-modification. The evaluator diagnostic is the interesting part: toxicity-similarity scalarizations, a multi-generator analysis and two general-purpose LLM judges reproduce parts of the aggregate tendency but fail to recover the stratified contrast at all.

tail.title: Know It, Act on It: Investigating Memory Utilization in LLM Personalization
tail.summary: Separates remembering from using by administering paired Know and Act tests on the same user preference: 16 systems, five memory architectures, 1,000 preferences embedded at three levels of expression strength. A large gap opens between the two, with agents passing the recall test for a preference yet failing to reflect that same preference in the paired behavioural scenario. Memory architectures narrow the gap but do not close it, and utilization is weakest precisely for health and therapy-related preferences, where failing to act carries the highest stakes.

tail.title: From Representations to Behaviors: Exploring the Person-Situation-Behavior Triad in LLMs
tail.summary: Adapts Funder's personality triad to LLM analysis: Person as internal representations, Situation as trait-affording contexts, Behavior as response patterns on social tasks. Using contrastive behaviour pairs grounded in shared situations, the authors identify sparse internal features associated with opposing trait poles through SAE decomposition, then validate trait relevance via effects on situational behaviour, token-level activation patterns and paraphrase robustness. Feature-level interventions induce bidirectional trait shifts across a separate diverse set of situations while preserving response validity, and applying the same interventions to social-intelligence tasks reproduces benefit-tradeoff patterns known from human personality research. Mechanistic evidence that LLMs carry controllable trait-like representations, not just conditioned outputs.

tail.title: Setoka: A Benchmark for Hierarchical User Understanding in Personalized Agents over Heterogeneous Data
tail.summary: Grounded in cognitive and personality psychology, Setoka defines four levels of user understanding (semantic memory, episodic memory, behaviour pattern, personality trait) and uses a psychometrics-based pipeline to synthesize coherent heterogeneous user data and queries at scale while preserving privacy. Evaluating 3 language models crossed with 5 memory systems over 10 synthetic users, performance is strong on semantic-memory retrieval, declines on episodic memory, and declines further still on behaviour-pattern and personality-trait tasks that require integrating fragmented information dispersed over time. Existing memory benchmarks measure fact retrieval and mistake it for user understanding.

tail.title: Human-LLM Collaborative Inductive Coding for Conceptualizing K-12 Educator AI Use
tail.summary: A procedural account of a multi-phase pipeline that adapted open, axial and selective coding to build a hierarchical codebook from 45,000 educator-to-AI messages, with LLMs generating candidate labels and structured annotations at scale while humans retained authority over category definitions and merging decisions. The instrument was then tested by three trained coders on an independent 2,560-message sample, with reliability established through iterative calibration using set-valued agreement measures appropriate to multi-label annotation, and extended with five codes the LLM phases never surfaced. Final codebook: 72 items, 19 categories, six domains. Explicitly treats the LLM as a labeling instrument rather than an interpretive agent.

tail.title: One Human, N Agents: Audit-Budget Allocation for LLM Agent Fleets under Miscalibrated, Correlated Confidence
tail.summary: Models one human auditing N LLM agents with budget B much smaller than N, guided by self-reported confidence that may be adversarially miscalibrated and by correlated errors, as budgeted noisy inspection over a two-level Gaussian copula. It locates the miscalibration threshold past which confidence-ranked auditing is worse than random, and two intuitions reverse: the threshold rises as the budget shrinks, and cross-family correlation is not low because shared task difficulty dominates model lineage. Five open-weight LLMs show operationally useless near-constant confidence with point estimates at or beyond the flip; one proprietary model is informative and lands below it. Gives a quantitative criterion for oversight that is vacuous.

tail.title: From Process to Evidence: How Computing Can Ground Appropriate Reliance on Legal AI
tail.summary: Analyzes the official record of the New York court system after more than 1,500 cases involving AI hallucinations in filings. The documents repeatedly call for evidence that does not exist (error rates, do-not-use lists) and substitute procedure in its place: training mandates, checklists, uncalibrated human review. Legal aid programs are told to track their own error rates and judges are left improvising their own tests, so the burden falls hardest on those least equipped to bear it. Maps legal duties onto the HCI concept of appropriate reliance and derives a computing research agenda of task taxonomies, shared error metrics, maintained benchmarks and test harnesses that work on private data.

tail.title: A Human-Centered Validation of the Explainability-Performance Coefficient
tail.summary: Proposes the EPC score, a model-agnostic metric quantifying explanation quality by explicitly balancing feature-selection sparsity against preserved model performance, and validates it empirically across tabular, text and image modalities. The score surfaces operational dependencies among network activations, data dimensionality and explainer performance, and is then checked against independent human-produced explanations, with higher EPC aligning with human lexical sentiment judgments and spatial visual annotations. One of the few XAI metric papers that closes the loop to human ground truth rather than stopping at a proxy.

tail.title: Would You Walk to the Car Wash? Revealing the Salience Bias of Large Language Models in Commonsense Reasoning
tail.summary: The SaliTrap benchmark spans four trap dimensions in which useless explicit distractors (for example numerical values) hijack models into ignoring implicit commonsense prerequisites. All 12 evaluated state-of-the-art LLMs suffer significantly, with severity scaling with distractor density, and detecting the trap turns out to be decoupled from actually avoiding it. The diagnostic result is the good one: re-eliciting the same models with the task framing stripped away recovers over 90% of the sycophantic-compliance failures, so the requisite knowledge is present and actively crowded out rather than absent. Lightweight inference-time prompting substantially closes the gap with no retraining, relocating the bottleneck from competence to elicitation.

tail.title: Beyond Borrowed Histories: Person-Aligned User Simulation for Interactive Role-Playing Evaluation
tail.summary: PALATE attacks two design flaws in role-play benchmarks: continuing a fixed dialogue history confounds the agent's own ability with the borrowed history, and a fixed rubric detached from the user need not track user satisfaction. It trains five per-user simulators that engage candidate agents in free-form multi-turn conversation over a frozen panel drawn from 300 character profiles, and pairs a general quality rubric with personalized rubrics. On held-out annotated data the personalized rubrics agree with human judgments better than the general rubric. Across 16 candidates it reports generic turn quality, long-horizon session capability and per-user experience separately rather than compressing to one user-independent ranking.

tail.title: ClawTrack: Towards Trace-Level Evaluation and Improvement of Real-World Autonomous Agents
tail.summary: A dual-assessment benchmark measuring what an agent achieves (Task Score) alongside how it achieves it (Process Score): 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services, and a Process Grader scoring each reasoning turn on goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization and result verification, anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items. Across 21 models and 16,000+ trials, process scores filter lucky passes invisible to outcome-only evaluation, the four dimensions prove complementary with result verification as the systematic bottleneck, and the framework is robust to judge-LLM choice. Process-based trajectory filtering also yields consistent post-training gains across model scales.

tail.title: Benchmarking Frontier Large Language Models Against Official Crash Database Coding Using Police Crash Narratives
tail.summary: A clean cautionary benchmark: 5,587 Arkansas fatal-crash narratives linked to 5,889 structured records (2015-2025) yielding 4,194 matched crashes, with six frontier LLMs coding crash manner, non-motorist relation, intersection type, work-zone relation, surface condition and light condition under an identical zero-shot prompt. Scored on agreement, macro-F1, Cohen's kappa, coverage and selective agreement against always-majority, always-Unknown and keyword-rule baselines with repeated-measures and GEE analyses. GPT-5.5 High led the LLMs, but the always-majority baseline produced higher raw agreement and the keyword-rule baseline matched the best LLM on macro-F1 and kappa. Differences across attributes exceeded differences across models.

tail.title: Subtract or Replay? Exact Deletion from Language-Model Memory
tail.summary: Argues exact deletion is a property of memory representation, not an algorithm. Replacing Gemma 3's global-attention layers with support-vector memory, algebraic decrement and retained-key refit agree at the next-token output to median KL 5.4e-15 over 31 support-token deletions at 1B, with +2.0% perplexity versus a matched fine-tune, and a masked-refit proxy is indistinguishable from the never-ingested floor under elicitation, relearning, sampling and LiRA attacks; utility cost rises to 11.2% at 4B and 44.3% at 12B. In a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid, additive writes admit a fixed decrement but the delta rule makes 12-49% of a record's contribution suffix-dependent, so checkpointed rewind-and-replay is needed, matching never-ingested logits and recurrent states bit for bit on real clinical records at contexts up to 18,842 tokens.

tail.title: When Specifications Conflict: A Symmetry-Based Framework for Measuring LLM Preferences
tail.summary: A controlled framework for observing how models resolve conflicts between competing instructions, using explicit conflicts plus a symmetry-based design that cancels confounds so preferences across representation types can be compared directly. On an executable mathematical benchmark with 550 conflict instances across 11 function families, four representation types produce a consistent ordering rather than random behaviour: formal language and naturalized formal language beat pure natural language, which beats input-output examples, with example effects further dependent on model capability and function family. Extended to heterogeneous conflicts in Boolean algebra, code generation and the clinical domain.

tail.title: RepBench: Compiling Benchmarks into Capability Representations for Large Language Models
tail.summary: Replaces paper-specific synthetic probe data with a benchmark-grounded layer: crawling 13,427 benchmark papers yields 182 capability clusters in 13 families, and harvesting 353 public benchmark datasets yields 46,149 audited probe texts covering 94 capabilities, each supported by at least two independent benchmarks. Raw per-text vectors show no natural cluster granularity while benchmark-pooled capability vectors show an interior clustering optimum on all 12 evaluated models, with low agreement to the human taxonomy. Under cross-benchmark transfer, difference-in-means attains the highest model-level mean on ten models while logistic regression wins the most capability-model cells, showing readout method and aggregation criterion are themselves evaluation dimensions.

tail.title: FriendBench: Benchmarking Dyadic Familiarity Inference in Humans and Multimodal Large Language Models
tail.summary: Infers from a 20-second clip of a dyadic ice-breaker conversation whether two people already know each other or are meeting as strangers, with every pair answering the same prompt type so only manner of interaction can reveal the answer. Across text, audio and video, 26 models from seven companies are compared against matched human panels over 96 balanced dyads. The best model and the human crowd are statistically indistinguishable on accuracy in every modality but get there differently: humans stay balanced across the two answers while the strongest models lean toward stranger, a difference in effective prior rather than discrimination. Only humans gain from visible behaviour on top of speech.

tail.title: Demystifying Entropy-based Selection for Chain-of-Thought Compression in Large Reasoning Models
tail.summary: A clean negative result: entropy-based pruning of CoT steps offers no advantage over random pruning in any evaluated setting, across various models and reasoning tasks. Moving from sentences to tokens, retaining low-entropy tokens appears to work only on mathematical benchmarks, and that is an artefact of numeric tokens being inherently low-entropy while also carrying the semantic content in those problems. Patching a small subset of CoT tokens with their original activations recovers near-perfect full-trace performance, giving causal evidence that task information is distributed across the whole reasoning chain rather than concentrated in heuristically identifiable tokens.

tail.title: Evidence-Type Competition: When Can Interventional Data Teach Language Models Causal Direction?
tail.summary: In Simpson's-paradox synthetic worlds where correlation and causal effect have opposite signs, raising the fraction of interventional samples in pretraining does not improve causal direction: the magnitude of the do()-response grows monotonically while its sign is copied from the observational context. What governs use of interventional evidence is the evidence type present at inference. Under identical training, a purely observational context induces systematic sign reversal in 29/50 worlds, a mixed context in 19/50, while aligned interventional probes alone yield 41/50 correct; erasing observational evidence releases the suppressed ability. Suppression is stable across seeds and persists at 0.93B parameters (31.8% vs 6% reversals), and activation patching localizes the switch to middle-layer observational rows. The capability lives in the weights, the switch lives in the context.

tail.title: Knowing When to Quit: Diagnosing and Training LLMs to Abort Futile Reasoning
tail.summary: Characterizes futile reasoning, where models generate expensive but semantically void derivations on beyond-capability tasks, and finds universal capability overreach plus systematic miscalibration between capability and behaviour. The dominant failure mode is specious reasoning that looks superficially valid but contains subtle errors, and it escalates with task difficulty, which is exactly the regime in which plausible-sounding wrong derivations mislead users. CaRL aligns behaviour to capability boundaries via reward shaping that incentivizes refusal over futile reasoning plus hindsight refusal augmentation converting failures into refusal supervision, substantially reducing futile reasoning while preserving task performance.

tail.title: When Derived Measurements Mislead: Quantifying and Mitigating LLM Over-Trust with Privileged-Modality Reliability Evidence
tail.summary: Defines derived-feature over-trust as an LLM granting a derived measurement the epistemic status of a direct fact or using it outside its valid scope, and operationalizes it with five estimands: conflict over-trust rate, context-induced error rate, correct repair rate, evidence-specific repair margin and utility harm rate. Demonstrated on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records where ECG supplies supervision but is never shown to the model, with one arm testing acceptance of a PPG rhythm contradicted by offline ECG and another testing rejection of a confirmed-reliable rhythm under misleading severe history. On a protocol-locked 187-patient test the baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 points with all paired CIs excluding zero, at a 0.67-point increase in unnecessary verification.

tail.title: Selecting Open-Weight Language Models for Zero-Shot Intent Classification: A Systematic Evaluation of 41 Models
tail.summary: 41 open-weight models across 15 families and the 135M-9B range, evaluated zero-shot on eight English intent-classification datasets, going well past exact-match accuracy into confidence calibration, robustness to realistic input perturbations, statistical reliability of rankings, deployment efficiency and benchmark saturation. Instruction-tuned 3B models outperform several 7B base models; differences among leading models on MASSIVE are statistically indistinguishable under pairwise McNemar tests; SNIPS is saturated and no longer discriminates among current open-weight models; and instruction tuning's effect on calibration is inconsistent rather than uniformly harmful. A model-selection paper that actually does the significance testing.

tail.title: Validation Evidence in LLM Repair Agents: How Much of What Passes Actually Tests the Bug?
tail.summary: BSG-VA captures each validation command at its exact working-tree state, extracts a test-only patch and replays it on the buggy code, the candidate state and the developer gold fix, assigning every event an evidence role from bug-discriminating down to misleading. Across 3,730 events in 643 rollouts on 110 tasks, 46.0% of positive comparable events carry no bug-discriminating information, and 23.8% of baseline rollouts close with a patch whose entire positive evidence base is of that kind. A three-arm experiment shows bug-contrast feedback cuts evidence-inadequate closure by 7.8 points versus an attention-matched reminder (p = 0.0029) and raises bug-discriminating evidence by 7.4 points (p = 0.011), though both fall below the prespecified 10-point smallest effect of interest.

tail.title: ORCA-bench: How Ready Are Language Model Agents for Oncall?
tail.summary: 1,079 root-cause-analysis tasks over a live OpenTelemetry-instrumented microservice system exposing six days of metrics, logs and traces through real telemetry interfaces plus full source access, systematically varying report specificity, time-to-detection and co-occurring faults. Notable for judge hygiene: ground-truth symptoms are curated and signed off by expert SREs and the LLM-as-judge is independently re-scored by humans at weighted Cohen's kappa 0.90. Across five frontier agents the best RCA accuracy is 25.3% on Medium (realistic-input) tasks and 10.0% on Hard, the weakest model hallucinates an implausible root cause in 40% of reports, and removing source-code access degrades every metric.

tail.title: SERPO: Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization for Open-Ended Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
tail.summary: Test-time RL for open-ended generation, where answer voting fails because valid responses share no canonical form and no external reward model or stronger judge is available. SERPO closes a three-way loop: Good-Normal-Bad response evolution organizes maximally separated rollouts into ordered archives, rubric evolution retains only criteria that discriminate those archives, probabilistic criterion scoring converts verdict-token likelihoods into reward signals, and policy evolution optimizes the actor, with new rollouts refreshing archives and rubrics. Across two model configurations, two in-domain and four out-of-domain benchmarks it improves HealthBench and ResearchQA by up to 20.63 and 20.31 points and the six-benchmark macro-average by up to 8.06.

tail.title: Benchmarks Are Not Validation: A System-Level View of Financial LLM Applications
tail.summary: A position paper from industry practice validating GenAI applications inside financial institutions, arguing that benchmark scores, task accuracy and one-off qualitative reviews are not evidence of production readiness. It lays out a multi-layer validation view across data, model design, retrieval and generation performance, agent behaviour, governance and implementation, and is specific about where LLM-as-a-judge belongs and what controls it needs: multiple judges, rubrics, explicit agreement measurement and auditability checks. Names failure modes static benchmarks miss, including retrieval failures, unfaithful generation, tool misuse, escalation errors and operational instability, and closes with a research agenda on judge alignment protocols and lifecycle validation standards.

tail.title: Beyond Component Testing: Validating Agentic AI Systems
tail.summary: Synthesizes 257 papers spanning agent evaluation, software assurance, cyber-physical systems, runtime monitoring and regulatory guidance into a five-dimension taxonomy of validation concerns: behavioral, safety, temporal, regulatory and multi-agent. Mapping current approaches onto it exposes where the field actually is, with behavioral evaluation comparatively mature while temporal validity, runtime evidence maintenance, regulatory legibility and open-ended multi-agent assurance remain under-developed. Three cross-domain case studies (medical care, industrial operations, smart mobility) ground the taxonomy in documented failure patterns, and the research agenda centres on bounded-autonomy specifications, adversarial trajectory generation and audit-ready evidence structures.

tail.title: An Instrument to Evaluate Governance Proposals: AI Policy Analysis at Scale
tail.summary: A jurisdiction-agnostic framework for assessing AI governance proposals along multiple policy attributes, built by combining subject-matter-expert qualitative input with computational text analysis to design rubrics, then quantifying relative emphasis of policy objectives through comparative visualizations. Methodologically relevant beyond policy: it benchmarks commercial LLMs doing rubric-based analysis against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model with explicitly stated analytical assumptions, and makes attribute selection, rubric construction and weighting schemes visible so users can check whether the instrument's embedded priorities match their own.

tail.title: Semantics of Subterfuge: Benchmarking Legal Deception Detection Against General-domain State-of-the-Art
tail.summary: A unified empirical evaluation of automatic deception detection across seven datasets (two legal, five general-domain), comparing six fine-tuned transformer models against seven LLMs under four prompting strategies. Results show strong domain sensitivity: fine-tuned models dominate in data-rich general domains while few-shot LLMs stay competitive in low-resource legal settings. The result worth noting for prompt design is that chain-of-thought prompting often underperforms direct classification on this task, one more case where the reasoning scaffold costs rather than helps.

tail.title: (Towards) Scalable Reliable Automated Evaluation with Large Language Models
tail.summary: An evaluation framework built on pairwise comparisons of outputs by multiple LLMs to dilute single-model bias, with an Elo rating system producing stable interpretable rankings and adjustable agreement thresholds running from full unanimity to majority voting, letting you trade evaluation confidence against coverage explicitly. Demonstrated on competency profiles extracted from scientific abstracts, where automatically derived rankings correlate well with expert judgments. Reference-free, so it extends to domains that have no objective ground truth, which is where most judge work actually lives.

tail.title: Improving Mental Health Screening and Early Risk Detection in Spanish
tail.summary: Three Spanish foundational models adapted to the mental-health domain through domain-specific pre-training, plus Incremental Context Expansion, an automatic relabeling method for early detection that identifies the point at which cumulative social-media messages provide sufficient evidence of a disorder and generates more informative training samples from that point. Fine-tuned models trained on ICE samples improve state of the art on three Spanish benchmarks while reducing detection latency. All models released publicly, which matters given how thin non-English mental-health NLP resources remain.

tail.title: DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 live on OpenRouter at $0.09/$0.18 per M tokens
tail.summary: Slug deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731 went live 06:22 UTC on release day with 1,048,576 context, 65,536 max output, at $0.09/M input and $0.18/M output. That is roughly an order of magnitude below frontier pricing at full context, making it the obvious cost floor for large-N eval runs that need long inputs. The API now natively speaks the Responses API format, which may require adapter changes in existing pipelines. A 37% discount is currently showing on the discounted-models collection (effective ~$0.088/$0.176), but OpenRouter publishes no start or expiry date for it, so do not budget a run around that rate.

tail.title: OpenRouter adds a floating deepseek-v4-flash-latest alias — a reproducibility hazard
tail.summary: A moving-pointer alias appeared in the catalog as ~deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-latest, with specs and pricing identical to the pinned 0731 build (1M context, 65,536 output, $0.09/$0.18). The tilde is OpenRouter's alias marker. For any large-N eval this is a trap: the alias will silently re-target on DeepSeek's next build, which can shift model behavior mid-run and contaminate a dataset that looks internally consistent. Pin the -0731 slug in eval configs and treat the alias as chat-only convenience.

tail.title: MiniMax-H3 — open-weight omni-modal model generating 2K video with native stereo audio
tail.summary: MiniMax released H3 (Hailuo 3.0), a ~33B H3-Omni-Transformer (~13B of that in AdaLN branches) that ingests text, up to 9 images, 3 video clips and 3 audio clips and emits video with synchronized stereo audio at up to 2K and 15 seconds. Three-module pipeline: H3-Context-IR preprocessing, H3-Base at 768p, then H3-Regenerate-2K upscaling by in-context regeneration, with 3D MM-RoPE for spatial-temporal position. Reference serving is 4 GPUs at BF16 under SGLang, so 16GB single-card use will depend on community quants and the 768p base stage only. Released under the restrictive MiniMax H3 Community License with mandated content-moderation guardrails, not a true open license.

tail.title: ComfyUI v0.30.0 — RAM weight pinning, MiniMax-H3 support, cuDNN attention fallback
tail.summary: Memory management is the headline: weights now load into process RAM under an MRU policy using new pinning infrastructure, and gradients are explicitly disabled on diffusion models to cut overhead — both directly useful when juggling multiple checkpoints on a 16GB card. Adds MiniMax-H3 integration, int8 convrot embedding lookup, and PrunaVAED for a faster LTX2.3 decoder. Backend work includes expanding k/v tensors when GQA would otherwise force the slow math-attention path (a real and easily-missed speed trap), a cuDNN attention fallback on Linux when flash attention is unavailable, and an AMD flash-attention fix. Also patches a Windows swap-memory query error and an SVG preview security issue.

tail.title: llama.cpp b10228/b10231 — DeepSeek V4 MTP plus DSpark self-speculative decoding
tail.summary: b10228 combines DeepSeek V4 multi-token prediction with DSpark speculative decoding; b10231 (same day) adds DSpark sidecar auto-resolution so dspark models rank above dflash when no type is specified, carrying Markov head information. The structural point for a single-GPU stack is that this is self-speculation — you get speculative-decoding throughput without loading a separate draft model, which on a 16GB card would otherwise consume VRAM you cannot spare. Related housekeeping in b10212 and b10225 loads MTP tensors only when actually used, returning VRAM if you run these architectures without speculative decoding enabled.

tail.title: llama.cpp b10232 — DeepSeek V4 hyper-connection kernels, Metal only for now
tail.summary: Implements DeepSeek V4 hyper-connections (GGML_OP_DSV4_HC_COMB/_PRE/_POST) with SIMDgroup-optimized kernels and production Sinkhorn iterations. Important caveat that is easy to miss in the changelog noise: this is a Metal-path implementation and the CUDA port is not in yet, so it does nothing on an NVIDIA card today. Any DSV4 local-performance numbers circulating from Apple Silicon this week should not be assumed to transfer to a 5060 Ti until the CUDA kernels land — worth watching specifically.

tail.title: llama.cpp b10227 — dedicated Qwen3 chat parser with tool-call delimiter handling
tail.summary: Adds a purpose-built Qwen3 chat parser handling tagged thinking blocks and tool-call delimiters, fixing malformed tool-call parsing when serving Qwen3-family models with tools. Relevant if any local agent harness routes through llama-server with a Qwen3 model — previously the generic parser could mangle thinking/tool boundaries in ways that look like model failure rather than parser failure. Cheap upgrade with no VRAM cost.

tail.title: ExLlamaV3 v1.3.0 — DeepseekV3 architecture support and a second-tier CPU K/V cache
tail.summary: Adds preliminary DeepseekV3 architecture support (validated against JoyAI-LLM-Flash and Moonlight-16B-A3B; routing groups not implemented yet). The headline for 16GB is the second-tier CPU K/V cache with an improved eviction policy — it spills KV to system RAM instead of hard-failing at the context limit, which is the standard wall on 30B-class EXL3 quants on a 5060 Ti. Also fixes frequency/repetition penalties that were collapsing throughput at long context, adds the XTC sampler and token bans, and patches a safetensors loader vulnerability. If you are on Windows, take v1.2.1 (Jul 27) too, which fixed JIT compilation and CPU offload there.

tail.title: KridgeDookie Qwen3.6-27B-ABLITERATED-PHILADELPHIA-CLASS — 0/842 refusals, undisclosed method
tail.summary: 27.36B abliterated Qwen3.6-27B under Apache-2.0, 2,504 downloads, retaining the base hybrid text-and-vision architecture — the only multimodal candidate in this week's abliteration crop. It carries the largest refusal screen of any card in the window: 0/842 refusals with 99.76% usable and zero degeneration, a held-out screen at 0/126 and 100% usable, and coherence regression 23/24 (95.83%). The card is candid that these are automated internal development evals, not standardized public leaderboards or independent audits. The gap worth noting for a PsychBench Abliterated context: largest eval in the window, and no named ablation technique whatsoever, so the result is not reproducible. Ships BF16 safetensors at 54.71GB and an unquantized text-only GGUF, so 16GB use waits on community quants.

tail.title: LongCat-Flash-Lite-Uncensored-Heretic — Magnitude-Preserving Orthogonal Ablation with published KL
tail.summary: Highest download count of any natively-new abliteration in the window (9,491) on Meituan's LongCat-Flash-Lite, 68.5B total with only ~2.9-4.5B activated (MoE), MIT licensed. Uses Heretic v1.4.0 with a Magnitude-Preserving Orthogonal Ablation (MPOA) variant targeting attn.o_proj and mlp.down_proj with per-layer direction indices — methodologically distinct in that it constrains weight-norm drift rather than doing plain directional projection. Publishes refusals 9/100 vs 100/100 baseline and KL divergence 0.1177, though that KL is 2.5x the best-in-class figure this week, so the accompanying 'preserving model quality' claim is weaker than it sounds and has no task-benchmark table behind it. Quants: Q2_K 24.2GB through BF16 138GB — too large for 16GB VRAM, but the extreme MoE sparsity makes CPU+RAM inference genuinely viable, and it is one of very few models here with a published KL to check your own numbers against.

tail.title: apetersson DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Abliterated-FP8 — benchmarks by proxy, and says so
tail.summary: Rank-1 refusal-direction projection on attention residual writers (lambda=3.5, k=1, layers 10-42) applied to the 304B MIT-licensed DSV4 Flash, in native mixed FP8_E4M3/BF16/F32; 2,314 downloads and 31 likes. It is the only card in the sweep citing named public benchmarks — UncensorBench (0 hard refusals, 200/200 keyword compliance), XSTest (0/450 refusals), StrongREJECT (0 hard refusals). The critical qualification is on the card itself: those numbers come from a quantized MLX derivative, not this checkpoint, and the author explicitly states direct behavioral benchmarking of the native-FP8 build has not been run and the results do not establish its refusal rate or demonstrate capability preservation. That disclosure is unusually rigorous for this corner of HF and makes it a good citation for how quantization/eval provenance gets laundered.

tail.title: apetersson DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Abliterated-DS4-Headroom128 — no behavioral eval at all
tail.summary: 1,971 downloads and 15 likes for a rank-1 residual-writer projection with FP8 fixed-point requantization, importing refusal directions from the drowzeys repo (lambda=3.5, layers 10-42, 36 tensors). 'Headroom128' denotes a quant profile tuned to fit a 128GB Apple Silicon box alongside the three-stage DSpark drafter: mixed GGUF v3 with IQ2_XXS at 44.34GiB, Q2_K at 28.22GiB, main model 86.72GiB plus DSpark 5.99GiB. Structural validation only — the card lists capability comparison and refusal-removal assessment as still required before making any quality claim, and calls itself an experimental low-bit model-surgery derivative. Nearly 2,000 people downloaded a model whose author says its refusal behavior is unmeasured.

tail.title: sakamakismile DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Abliterated-NVFP4 — ablation extended into the speculative drafter
tail.summary: 163.49GiB across 48 shards, MIT, 8 likes. Methodologically the most interesting variant of the DSV4 cluster: rank-1 refusal-direction projection at lambda=3.5 over layers 10-42 plus the MTP attention writers across all three DSpark stages, meaning the ablation reaches into the speculative-decode drafter that most repos leave stock. That matters because an unablated drafter proposing refusal tokens is a plausible source of the residual refusal other cards report. No behavioral eval: the card cleanly separates what was measured (structural validation, coherence on three probes) from what was not (throughput, DSpark acceptance rate, benchmarks, behavioral validation of this artifact), and notes synthetic amax was used for activation scales instead of real-traffic calibration, with unknown quality impact.

tail.title: huihui-ai DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-abliterated-GGUF — highest visibility, zero measurement
tail.summary: 284B MIT-licensed GGUF set with 41 likes, produced with Sumandora's remove-refusals-with-transformers — a tool the card itself quotes as a crude, proof-of-concept implementation for removing refusals without TransformerLens. There is no eval of any kind; the only quality statement is qualitative, that Q4 used a stronger ablation intensity than Q2 so the rejection rate was smaller. huihui-ai is the highest-volume abliteration publisher on HuggingFace and publishes essentially nothing measurable, which is the cleanest illustration of the window's inverse relationship between reported rigor and adoption. Their Qwen3.6-27B abliterated GGUFs (Q2_K 10.9GB, Q6_K 22.4GB, Q8_0 29GB, F16 54.7GB) are the practical size reference for 16GB fit.

tail.title: Uniboshi Kimi-K3-Abliterated-V1 — structural metric presented as a behavioral one
tail.summary: Abliteration of the 2.8T Kimi K3 under the kimi-k3 license, 118 downloads and 35 likes, with three near-identical forks appearing in-window. The eval is a table of safeguard removal percentages of 98.44-98.62% across .down_proj, .o_proj, .embed_tokens and routed_expert_up_proj. That measures how much weight was changed, not what the model does — a reader skimming sees a high percentage and infers a refusal rate. Worth logging as a specimen of the window's dominant failure mode: weight-delta metrics dressed as behavioral evidence. Entirely out of reach locally at 2.8T.

tail.title: Anthropic brings MCP 2026-07-28 to Claude, rolling out in phases
tail.summary: Confirms the new spec is live and that support is rolling out across Claude products, i.e. phased rather than immediate, with no completion date given. Worth watching for anyone running local MCP servers, since a stateless-core migration will eventually change how those get configured. Notable adjacent data point: Claude Code has published nothing since 2.1.220 on 2026-07-24, a roughly ten-day gap against a prior near-daily cadence, which may or may not be related to absorbing this migration.

tail.title: OpenAI Agents SDK for Python v0.19.2 — MCP credential redaction and session fixes
tail.summary: Patch release improving credential redaction in MCP error messages (a real leak vector when agent errors get logged), cleaning up the MCP transport layer, fixing item-counting across SQLite/SQLAlchemy/MongoDB/Redis/Dapr session backends, and correcting voice audio-dispatcher and iterator-cancellation behavior plus monotonic export deadlines in tracing. The more consequential release is the preceding v0.19.0 (2026-07-27), which introduced Programmatic Tool Calling — letting supported models emit JavaScript to coordinate tool calls — along with a VercelCloudBucketMountStrategy for mounted sessions.

tail.title: Qwen3.7 Flash on OpenRouter at $0.03/$0.13 per M — cheapest million-token context available
tail.summary: Predates the window but surfaced during the catalog sweep and is directly relevant to eval-pipeline economics: 1,000,000 context at $0.03/M input and $0.13/M output, roughly 3x cheaper on input than DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 and the cheapest million-token option in the catalog. For large-N runs where per-item input dominates cost (long prompts, short structured outputs) this is the current floor. The tradeoff is capability class — verify on a pilot subset against your rubric before committing a full run, since AA has not published a comparable index score for it.

tail.title: Thinking Machines Inkling Small appears on OpenRouter
tail.summary: First Thinking Machines entry in the OpenRouter catalog, added 20:25 UTC Jul 30: 524,288 context at $0.50/M input and $1.20/M output. Roughly 5x the input price of DeepSeek V4 Flash with half the context, so it is not a volume-eval candidate — but it is the first time this lab's weights are reachable through a standard routing layer, which matters for cross-vendor comparison sets. Artificial Analysis benchmarked it Jul 30; check that score before assuming the price premium buys capability.

tail.title: Anthropic Frontier Red Team on three real-world cybersecurity incidents
tail.summary: Frontier Red Team writeup investigating three real-world incidents surfaced through their cybersecurity evaluations. Relevant as eval-methodology material rather than as a release: it is one of the few published accounts of a frontier lab tracing eval signals through to actual observed incidents, which is the validity link most capability evals never establish. Pairs with Anthropic's Jul 27 position statement on open-weights models, which is worth reading alongside the abliteration cluster in this brief given that refusal-ablated derivatives of MIT-licensed frontier MoEs are precisely the failure mode open-weight policy has to reckon with.

tail.title: llm-mcp-client 0.1a0 — connect Simon Willison's llm CLI to any MCP server
tail.summary: A plugin that lets the `llm` CLI act as an MCP client, so any MCP server becomes a tool available to whatever model llm is pointed at. Patrick could point this at his own memory and mimesis servers and script one-off pipeline steps from bash or a scheduled task, without spinning up a full Claude Code session — useful for the NewsBrief cron path where a cheap model just needs tool access.

tail.title: datasette-mcp — expose any SQLite database to an agent over MCP
tail.summary: A Datasette plugin adding an MCP endpoint with three tools: list_databases, get_database_schema, execute_sql. Patrick has a lot of research data sitting in SQLite and CSV; dropping it behind Datasette would give Claude Code natural-language SQL over PsychBench run tables or NewsBrief history without writing a bespoke server for each dataset.

tail.title: qm — Y Combinator's multiplayer agent harness, open sourced
tail.summary: YC released the agent runtime it runs internally: a headless TypeScript/Node core with Postgres for sessions and memory, per-user isolated sandboxes where installed tools persist between sessions, and a model-agnostic interface (Claude Code, OpenCode, Pi). It hit 665 points on HN. The interesting part for Patrick is the architecture rather than the product — persistent per-user sandboxes and a Postgres session/memory layer is a more industrial version of what his own agent stack does with files.

tail.title: Mu — 67 everyday internet tools behind a single MCP endpoint
tail.summary: A single Go binary that gives an agent news, web search, a real SMTP mail server with per-agent addresses, markets, weather, video, places, images, files, calendar and contacts — 67 tools, one MCP endpoint, installable via curl or Docker Compose. Instead of wiring five separate MCP servers into the NewsBrief pipeline, Patrick could point it at Mu and get search plus fetch plus mail-out in one config line; the per-agent email address alone is a neat trick for a scheduled agent that needs to report back.

tail.title: Wienerdog — file-based memory and self-improving skills for Claude Code
tail.summary: Gives Claude Code and Codex CLI a shared Obsidian-compatible markdown memory vault in PARA structure, plus a 'nightly dreaming' process that reviews the day's conversations, promotes learnings into persistent memory, and mints new skills out of workflows it saw repeated. Has a Windows PowerShell installer. This is a direct competitor to Patrick's own LKHS/auto-memory setup — worth reading for the nightly-consolidation design even if he doesn't install it, since skill-synthesis-from-repeated-workflows is something his stack doesn't do.

tail.title: Agent-Manager — a tmux TUI for running Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode side by side
tail.summary: Runs each agent in its own tmux session with a unified live-status list, a collapsible project tree, space-to-prompt-without-attaching, and Ctrl+R to open syntax-highlighted full-file diffs of what an agent changed — you can comment on lines and send the comments back as a review prompt. Sessions survive quitting the manager. For Patrick's parallel-subagent workflow this replaces alt-tabbing between terminals; Windows needs WSL2.

tail.title: Shellphone — MCP extension linking Claude chat and Claude Code
tail.summary: An MCP server that bridges a Claude.ai chat session to a running Claude Code instance on your machine, so you can kick off or steer local work from the web/mobile app. For Patrick this is the 'drive the desktop stack from my phone' piece — closer to what his conversate skill does for voice, but text-first and no browser app to keep open.

tail.title: PinFix — click any UI element and edit its source in Claude Code
tail.summary: A dev-server overlay: click on a rendered element in the browser and it resolves back to the source file and line, then hands that to Claude Code as the edit target. For the NewsBrief artifact and any HTML dashboards Patrick builds, this removes the 'which of these divs is that' round-trip entirely.

tail.title: Ski — on-device voice coding for Claude Code and Codex
tail.summary: Free, runs speech recognition locally rather than shipping audio to a cloud API, and pipes dictation straight into Claude Code or Codex. Patrick already has a local Whisper + Kokoro pipeline and a conversate skill; Ski is the lighter-weight version of the same idea for when he just wants to talk a prompt instead of typing it, and it's worth comparing against his own stack for latency.

tail.title: claudemon — play Pokémon while Claude Code thinks
tail.summary: Exactly what it says: a terminal Pokémon game that fills the dead air during long Claude Code runs. Pure delight, and a small honest commentary on what agentic coding actually feels like minute to minute. Zero adoption value, high 'someone actually built this' value.

tail.title: Claude MIDI Twister — an agent visualizer for a DJ MIDI controller
tail.summary: Maps Claude Code agent state onto the LED rings of a Midi Fighter Twister so you can see token burn, tool calls and agent activity as physical glowing knobs. The genuinely interesting move is treating agent telemetry as an ambient physical display rather than another terminal pane — a pattern Patrick could steal for his scheduled agents using any cheap MIDI or LED device.

tail.title: peri — a Rust coding agent that runs Claude Code plugins and skills
tail.summary: A from-scratch coding agent in Rust that is deliberately compatible with the Claude Code plugin and skill format, so the skills you already wrote keep working. Relevant to Patrick because it means his skill investments (mimesis, audio-overview, eval-methodology-playbook) are becoming portable artifacts rather than Anthropic-locked ones.

tail.title: Boris Cherny on trying to get Claude Code to rewrite the Claude app in Swift
tail.summary: Claude Code's creator on what happened when he pointed it at a full native rewrite of Anthropic's own app, via Gruber. Worth reading as an honest account of where agentic coding hits its ceiling on large real codebases from someone with no incentive to undersell it — a useful calibration point against the demo-driven claims elsewhere.

tail.title: Karpathy's Pelican
tail.summary: Karpathy weighing in on the pelican-on-a-bicycle SVG benchmark, at 491 points on HN. The recurring joke-benchmark has quietly become the most-watched informal capability test in the field, and the thread is a good snapshot of where the frontier models actually land on spatial reasoning through code.

tail.title: WASTE — run Kimi K3 in 29GB of RAM by streaming experts off NVMe
tail.summary: A dependency-free C inference engine that exploits MoE sparsity: only ~4% of experts fire per token, so it keeps the shared trunk resident in RAM and streams individual 3-bit experts from disk, with a lookahead router prefetching next-layer experts and spare RAM used as a bounded expert cache. Gets ~0.5-0.6 tok/s on a 64GB MacBook. Slow, but it reframes the constraint from VRAM to storage bandwidth — directly relevant to Patrick's 16GB 5060 Ti ceiling if CUDA support lands. Needs ~1TB free NVMe for the converted container.

tail.title: Isopolis — an isometric pixel map of San Francisco
tail.summary: A hand-crafted isometric pixel-art rendering of the entire city, pannable in the browser. The kind of long-haul solo craft project that AI tooling hasn't made easier and probably can't — a nice counterweight to a feed otherwise full of agent harnesses.

tail.title: ssh ssh.place
tail.summary: The whole product is a hostname you SSH into. Terminal-native toys are having a moment and this one is a clean demo of how much interface you can deliver over a protocol nobody thinks of as a UI layer.

tail.title: Make your Framework 12 sound like a creaky door
tail.summary: Reads the Framework laptop's hinge angle sensor and plays a proportional creaking-door sound as you open the lid. Perfectly useless, perfectly executed. File under things that make hardware hacking look fun again.

tail.title: An AI wrote and illustrated a book of fables about threads and packets
tail.summary: A daily-generated illustrated fable series where the moral lessons are about concurrency primitives and network protocols. It's the good version of AI-generated creative output: a tight, weird constraint that a human chose, rather than open-ended slop. Interesting to Patrick as a format experiment more than as writing.

tail.title: AI-generated poster wins the Ohio State Fair contest
tail.summary: A state fair art contest awarded first place to an AI-generated poster, and the ensuing HN argument (124 points) is the whole cultural fight in miniature — disclosure rules, what juried competition is for, and whether the judges could tell. A cleaner test case than the usual gallery-scandal story because the stakes are small and the institution is unglamorous.

tail.title: Scalzi: Another reason not to use AI for your writing
tail.summary: The third working novelist in the same week to publish on this, which is itself the story. Scalzi's angle is craft-formation rather than ethics: the argument that the drafting struggle is where the writer gets made. Short, and the comment threads on his blog are usually better than the HN ones.

tail.title: Agent skill that forces docs into ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English
tail.summary: A Claude Code skill enforcing the aerospace industry's controlled-language standard: approved vocabulary, one topic per sentence, mandatory active voice. 334 points on HN. Beyond the aviation use case, this is a clean worked example of a skill that enforces a hard style spec rather than nudging — the same architecture Patrick's mimesis fingerprint gate uses, from the opposite direction.

tail.title: condense-json 1.0 — shrink JSON logs by deduplicating repeated strings
tail.summary: Replaces duplicate strings in a JSON document with a reference syntax, built specifically for the SQLite logs the llm tool generates. Patrick's NewsBrief run directories and LKHS transcript exports have exactly this shape — enormous repeated system prompts and boilerplate — so this is a cheap size win on any archive of agent conversations he keeps.

tail.title: datasette-agent 0.4a0 — agent tools that execute JavaScript in your browser
